Unit 3 • SL

Data Structures & Logic

Introduction

How do we organise data so we can find it quickly and use it efficiently?

This unit focuses on the transition from single-item variables to collections. You will explore how data is structured in memory to improve efficiency in both time (speed of access) and space (memory usage). Key paradigms include Static vs Dynamic structures, and the rules of LIFO and FIFO.

You'll begin by comparing rigid arrays with flexible lists. Then, you'll master two fundamental abstract data types: the Stack (like a pile of trays) and the Queue (like a line for lunch), learning how to manipulate them and apply them to real-world problems.

Static vs Dynamic Structures

Data structures differ in how they manage memory:

  • Static (e.g., Array): Fixed size, contiguous memory (items next to each other). Fast access but wasteful if not full.
  • Dynamic (e.g., List): Resizable, non-contiguous memory. Flexible but can be slower to access specific items directly.

The Stack (LIFO)

A Stack is a LIFO (Last In, First Out) structure. Imagine a stack of plates — you can only add or remove the top one.

  • Push: Add an item to the top.
  • Pop: Remove the top item.
  • Peek: Look at the top item without removing it.

Real-world use: The "Undo" button in your text editor.

The Queue (FIFO)

A Queue is a FIFO (First In, First Out) structure. Imagine a queue for a bus — the first person to arrive is the first to board.

  • Enqueue: Add an item to the rear.
  • Dequeue: Remove an item from the front.

Real-world use: A printer buffer (first document sent is first printed).

1D & 2D Lists

We use lists to store multiple related items under one name. A 2D List (or Matrix) is a list of lists, useful for grids, game boards, or images.

2D Indices Trick

Remember "RC Cola": Row then Column. grid[row][col] accesses the item at that position.

Key Terminology
TermDefinition
Static StructureA data structure with a fixed size determined at compile time (e.g., an array).
Dynamic StructureA data structure that can grow or shrink in size during execution (e.g., a linked list or Python list).
LIFOLast In, First Out. The principle used by Stacks.
FIFOFirst In, First Out. The principle used by Queues.
Push / PopOperations to add/remove items from the TOP of a stack.
Enqueue / DequeueOperations to add to the REAR and remove from the FRONT of a queue.
PointerA variable that stores the memory address of another value (used to track Top/Front/Rear).
OverflowAttempting to push an item onto a full stack.
UnderflowAttempting to pop an item from an empty stack.

Common Misconceptions

Direct vs Sequential

Thinking you can 'jump' to any item in a dynamic list instantly. Often, the computer must walk through the list item-by-item to find it.

Stack Direction

Trying to remove items from the bottom of specific stacks. LIFO means the bottom is stuck until the top is gone!

2D Array Indices

Confusing [x][y] with [row][col]. In programming, we usually index by [row] (vertical position) then [col] (horizontal position).

Real-World Uses

  • Undo/Redo features (Stacks)
  • Browser history (Stacks)
  • Printer job spooling (Queues)
  • Keyboard buffers (Queues)
  • Music playlists (Lists)

Think Deeper

"How does structure dictate knowledge?" Does the way we organise data change what we can know about it? (e.g., finding a value in a sorted list vs an unsorted pile).
